events.title: Seneca relegated to Corsica
events.summary: In 41 Messalina procured the condemnation of Caligula's sister Julia Livilla for adultery with Seneca; Livilla was exiled and killed, and Seneca spent eight years relegated on Corsica until Agrippina recalled him in 49 to tutor Nero.
events.detail: From exile Seneca wrote the Consolation to Helvia (his mother), which presents banishment as a Stoic indifferent, and the Consolation to Polybius, a fawning appeal to Claudius's freedman that he later preferred to forget. On his recall he was made praetor and, with Burrus, guided the first years of Nero's reign.

events.title: Revolt of Aedemon and the conquest of Mauretania
events.summary: After Caligula's murder of king Ptolemy (40), the royal freedman Aedemon raised Mauretania in revolt; Roman forces needed until 42-44 to suppress it, after which Claudius organised the kingdom as two procuratorial provinces, Caesariensis and Tingitana.
events.detail: Inscriptions from Volubilis honour the local notable Marcus Valerius Severus, who led auxiliaries against Aedemon and obtained for his town Roman citizenship, municipal status and tax remission (44). Gnaeus Hosidius Geta twice defeated the Moorish chief Salabus in 42, nearly dying of thirst until a native's rain-making ritual saved his army (Dio). The provinces were each governed by an equestrian procurator with auxiliary garrisons.

events.title: Suetonius Paullinus crosses the Atlas
events.summary: In 42 Gaius Suetonius Paullinus, as legate in Mauretania, became the first Roman commander to cross the Atlas, marching ten days beyond the range to the river Ger through black dust deserts and forests full of elephants and snakes.
events.detail: Pliny the Elder, who read Paullinus's own account, preserves the details: snow on the summits even in summer, forests of unknown trees and the Canarii tribes who ate dog meat. Paullinus later commanded in Britain (58-61) and against Boudica, and fought for Otho in 69.

events.title: Agrippa I executes James son of Zebedee
events.summary: Shortly before his death in 44, Agrippa I had the apostle James, son of Zebedee, beheaded and imprisoned Peter, who escaped; Acts presents Agrippa's sudden death at Caesarea as divine punishment.
events.detail: Josephus and Acts both describe Agrippa dying after being hailed as a god at games in Caesarea, wearing a robe of silver that shone in the morning sun. Agrippa's attack on the Jerusalem church fits his cultivation of Jewish piety (Mishnah Sotah 7.8 remembers him weeping at the reading of the law). After 44 the leadership of the Jerusalem community passed to James the brother of Jesus.

events.title: Claudius's British triumph
events.summary: Claudius celebrated his triumph over Britain in 44 after only sixteen days on the island, climbing the Capitoline steps on his knees; he took the name Britannicus for his infant son, and arches were voted at Rome and Gesoriacum.
events.detail: Governors who had won triumphal ornaments marched in the procession, and Messalina followed in a carriage. A naval crown was hung beside the civic crown on the Palatine to mark the conquest of the Ocean. The Arch of Claudius on the Via Flaminia, part of the Aqua Virgo, was dedicated in 51-52; its inscription records the surrender of eleven British kings "without any loss". Aulus Plautius received an ovation in 47, the last given to a non-imperial general.

events.title: Claudius announces in advance the eclipse of his birthday
events.summary: Expecting a solar eclipse on his birthday, 1 August 45, Claudius issued an edict in advance explaining its time, extent and causes so that it would not be taken as an evil omen.
events.detail: Dio quotes the edict as explaining that the moon, passing under the sun, blocks its light. The annular eclipse of 1 August 45 was indeed visible in the Mediterranean. The episode reflects Claudius's scholarly bent and the political danger of portents, which had been used against emperors.

events.title: The prophet Theudas killed by Fadus
events.summary: Under the procurator Cuspius Fadus (44-46) the prophet Theudas led a large crowd with their possessions to the Jordan, promising to part its waters; Fadus's cavalry killed many and Theudas's head was brought to Jerusalem.
events.detail: Theudas is one of several "sign prophets" Josephus describes, who promised Exodus-style miracles; Acts 5.36 puts a Theudas before Judas the Galilean, a chronological error. Fadus's successor Tiberius Julius Alexander, an apostate Jew, crucified James and Simon, sons of Judas the Galilean.

events.title: Famine in Judaea and the aid of Queen Helena of Adiabene
events.summary: During a severe famine in Judaea c. 46-48, Queen Helena of Adiabene, a convert to Judaism, bought grain in Egypt and figs in Cyprus for the people of Jerusalem, and her son King Izates sent money; Acts records famine relief sent from the Antioch church by Barnabas and Paul.
events.detail: The famine is one of several food crises under Claudius. Helena built a palace in Jerusalem and the monumental "Tomb of the Kings" north of the city, where a sarcophagus inscribed "Queen Sadan" has been identified as hers. The royal house of Adiabene, a Parthian vassal on the Tigris, sent soldiers to fight for the rebels in 66.

events.title: Paul and Barnabas's mission to Cyprus and Galatia
events.summary: Sent out by the church of Antioch c. 46-48, Paul and Barnabas preached in Cyprus, where Acts says they won over the proconsul Sergius Paullus, and in the cities of southern Galatia, establishing mixed communities of Jews and Gentiles.
events.detail: The journey (the "first journey" of Acts 13-14) is not mentioned explicitly in Paul's letters, which refer only to work in Syria and Cilicia. An inscription from Pisidian Antioch naming a Lucius Sergius Paullus and others from Cyprus support the plausibility of the proconsul. The admission of uncircumcised Gentiles provoked the dispute settled at Jerusalem.
events.locName: Cyprus, Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Derbe

events.title: Claudius's Secular Games for the 800th year of Rome
events.summary: In 47, while censor, Claudius celebrated Secular Games for Rome's 800th year by the Varronian count, only 64 years after Augustus's, and was mocked for inviting people to games no one had seen or would see again when many present had seen those of 17 BC.
events.detail: The Troy Game in the Circus featured Britannicus and the young Lucius Domitius (Nero), whose louder reception Tacitus treats as a sign of things to come. A phoenix was exhibited in the Comitium (Pliny). Claudius also extended the pomerium in 49 to include the Aventine, recorded on surviving cippi, justified by the conquest of Britain.

events.title: Death of Valerius Asiaticus
events.summary: In 47 Messalina, coveting the Gardens of Lucullus, had the Narbonensian ex-consul Decimus Valerius Asiaticus, twice consul and a leader in the plot against Caligula, accused of adultery and of sedition among the troops; Claudius tried him in his bedchamber and he opened his veins.
events.detail: Asiaticus, from Vienna in Narbonensis, was the first Gallic senator to hold two consulships; Claudius's Lyon speech the next year sneers at him as a "robber" from Vienna. Tacitus has him ask that his pyre be moved so as not to scorch his trees. The case is the classic example of Messalina's influence and Claudius's private trials (intra cubiculum).

events.title: Ostorius Scapula disarms the tribes; first Iceni revolt
events.summary: Arriving in 47, Publius Ostorius Scapula ordered the disarming of suspect tribes south of the Trent and Severn; the Iceni, allies until then, rose with their neighbours and were defeated storming an earthwork, where Ostorius's son won the civic crown.
events.detail: Tacitus says Ostorius used only auxiliaries. Prasutagus probably owed his client kingship to the aftermath. Ostorius then campaigned against the Deceangli and the Brigantes and turned against the Silures and Caratacus. The disarming policy, with its humiliation of a client people, prefigured the Boudican revolt of 60.

events.title: Claudius adds three letters to the Latin alphabet
events.summary: As censor in 47 Claudius introduced three new letters: the inverted digamma (for consonantal u), the antisigma (for ps or bs) and a half H (for the sound between i and u, as in optumus/optimus).
events.detail: Tacitus (11.13-14) links the reform to Claudius's antiquarian learning. The letters appear on public inscriptions of his reign (the inverted digamma most often, as in AMPLIAVIT written with it) and were abandoned after his death, which makes them a precise dating criterion for epigraphers. Claudius had published a book on the subject before becoming emperor.

events.title: The apostolic council at Jerusalem
events.summary: Around 48-49 Paul and Barnabas met the leaders of the Jerusalem church, James, Peter and John, who agreed that Gentile converts need not be circumcised; Paul was to go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised.
events.detail: Paul's own account (Galatians 2.1-10) says only that he was asked to remember the poor, the origin of his later collection for Jerusalem. Acts 15 adds the "apostolic decree" requiring Gentiles to abstain from idol meat, blood, strangled animals and sexual immorality, which Paul never mentions. The subsequent "incident at Antioch", where Peter withdrew from table fellowship with Gentiles and Paul opposed him to his face, shows the question was not settled.
events.debate: Relationship between Galatians 2 and Acts 15 (and Acts 11.30) is disputed.

events.title: War in the Bosporus and the surrender of Mithridates
events.summary: When Mithridates VIII, deposed king of the Bosporus, tried to recover his throne from his brother Cotys I, Roman cohorts under Gaius Julius Aquila and allies of the Aorsi took the Dandarid town of Uspe in 49, massacring its inhabitants; Mithridates surrendered to the Aorsian king Eunones, who interceded for his life.
events.detail: Aulus Didius Gallus had installed Cotys c. 45-46. Tacitus describes the siege of Uspe with its wattle and earth walls and the slaughter that terrified the region. Mithridates was brought to Rome, where he addressed Claudius boldly ("I was not sent back, I came back"), and lived in Rome until Galba executed him in 68.

events.title: Paul in Philippi, Thessalonica and Corinth; 1 Thessalonians
events.summary: Around 49-51 Paul crossed to Macedonia, founding churches at Philippi and Thessalonica, and then spent eighteen months at Corinth, from where he wrote 1 Thessalonians, the earliest surviving Christian text, c. 50.
events.detail: At Corinth Paul worked as a tentmaker with Aquila and Prisca, Jews recently expelled from Rome by Claudius. Acts 18.12-17 has the Jews bring him before the proconsul Gallio, whose term the Delphi inscription dates to 51/52, the fixed point of Pauline chronology. Gallio dismissed the charge as a dispute over words and names in Jewish law. The letters to the Corinthians, written from Ephesus soon after, reveal a fractious community divided over leaders, sex, food offered to idols and spiritual gifts.

events.title: Radamistus seizes Armenia
events.summary: In 51 Radamistus, son of Pharasmanes of Iberia, invaded Armenia, besieged his uncle Mithridates in the fortress of Gorneae, bribed the Roman prefect of the garrison and murdered Mithridates and his family after swearing not to harm him "by sword or poison"; the legate Ummidius Quadratus did nothing.
events.detail: Tacitus treats the episode as a scandal of Roman inaction. Vologases I exploited it to install his brother Tiridates in Armenia (52-54), opening the war Corbulo fought under Nero. Radamistus's pregnant wife Zenobia, abandoned in the Araxes during his flight, was rescued by shepherds and treated as royalty by Tiridates.

events.title: Famine of 51 and Claudius mobbed in the Forum
events.summary: In 51 Rome was said to have only fifteen days' grain left; Claudius was pelted with crusts in the Forum and had to escape by a back door, and he responded with incentives for shipowners who would sail in winter.
events.detail: Suetonius (Claudius 18-19) lists the privileges: insurance against storm losses at state expense, exemption from the Papian-Poppaean marriage penalties for citizens, Latin rights to Latins and the ius trium liberorum to women who built ships of 10,000 modii capacity and carried grain to Rome for six years. The measures, together with the new harbour at Portus, show the state working through private shippers (navicularii).

events.title: Caratacus pardoned by Claudius
events.summary: Handed over in chains by Cartimandua of the Brigantes after his defeat in 51, Caratacus was paraded with his family before the people and praetorians; his dignified speech won pardon for himself and his family from Claudius, and they also paid homage to Agrippina on her own tribunal.
events.detail: Tacitus gives him a speech arguing that his resistance made Claudius's victory glorious and that mercy would be an eternal witness to his clemency. Dio adds that, seeing Rome, he asked why those who had such possessions coveted British huts. Tacitus notes the novelty of a woman presiding over Roman standards.

events.title: Senatus consultum Claudianum
events.summary: A decree of 52, proposed by Claudius and drafted by his freedman Pallas, provided that a free woman who cohabited with another's slave against his master's will became, after three warnings, the master's slave herself, and her children slaves.
events.detail: Pallas was rewarded with the praetorian insignia and 15 million sesterces, which he refused, and the Senate inscribed its thanks on a bronze tablet beside the statue of Julius Caesar, an honour Pliny the Younger later found outrageous. The decree, aimed at protecting masters' property in slaves' offspring, remained law until Justinian repealed it.

events.title: The Silures defeat a legion; death of Ostorius Scapula
events.summary: After Caratacus's capture the Silures continued the war, killing a camp prefect and eight centurions, routing foraging parties and defeating a legion under Manlius Valens; Ostorius Scapula died worn out by the struggle in 52, and his successor Aulus Didius Gallus found the province in turmoil.
events.detail: Ostorius had declared that the Silures' name must be blotted out like the Sugambri, which Tacitus says only made them fight harder. The Silures were finally subdued by Frontinus (74-77), who built the legionary fortress of Isca (Caerleon) in their territory.

sides.strength: legio II Augusta detachments under Manlius Valens

battle.significance: Showed that Caratacus's fall had not ended Welsh resistance.

events.title: Aqua Claudia and Anio Novus completed
events.summary: On 1 August 52 Claudius dedicated the two greatest aqueducts of Rome, begun by Caligula in 38: the Aqua Claudia (c. 69 km, from springs near Subiaco) and the Anio Novus (c. 87 km, from the Anio), carried together on a single arcade for the last stretch into the city.
events.detail: Frontinus gives their deliveries as 4,607 and 4,738 quinariae, the two largest in the system, and the cost as 350 million sesterces. Their monumental double crossing of the Via Labicana and Praenestina is the Porta Maggiore, with inscriptions recording restorations by Vespasian (71) and Titus (81). Nero built a branch (Arcus Neroniani) to the Caelian to supply the Domus Aurea.

events.title: Earliest military diplomas
events.summary: The earliest surviving military diploma, issued on 11 December 52 to a sailor of the Misene fleet, attests Claudius's practice of granting Roman citizenship and legal marriage (conubium) to non-citizen auxiliaries and sailors after 25 or more years' service.
events.detail: Diplomas were pairs of bronze tablets bound together, certified copies of a constitution posted in Rome (on the Capitol, later behind the temple of Divus Augustus). Over a thousand survive; their lists of units, governors and dates are a basic source for the provincial garrisons and fasti. Grants of citizenship to the children ended under Antoninus Pius c. 140, and diplomas faded out in the third century after the Constitutio Antoniniana.

events.title: Senate honours the freedman Pallas
events.summary: In 52 the Senate voted Claudius's financial secretary (a rationibus) Pallas the praetorian insignia and 15 million sesterces and inscribed its decree on bronze; he accepted only the honours, and his reputed fortune of 300 million made him a byword for freedman power.
events.detail: Pallas, a freedman of Antonia Minor who allegedly carried her warning about Sejanus to Tiberius, backed Agrippina's marriage to Claudius and Nero's adoption. His brother Felix became procurator of Judaea. Nero dismissed him in 55 and had him killed in 62 for his wealth. Pliny the Younger, finding the inscription on his tomb on the Via Tiburtina, wrote two indignant letters about it.

events.title: Claudius frees sick slaves abandoned on the Tiber island
events.summary: Claudius decreed that slaves abandoned by their masters on the Tiber island, at the temple of Aesculapius, to avoid the cost of treating them should become free (as Junian Latins) if they recovered, and that masters who killed sick slaves rather than abandoning them were liable for murder.
events.detail: Suetonius and the jurist Modestinus record the measure. The Tiber island sanctuary of Aesculapius, founded in 291 BC, remained a place of healing; the hospital of San Giovanni Calibita stands there today. The edict is one of several early imperial interventions limiting masters' powers that culminated under Hadrian and Antoninus Pius.
events.debate: Exact date unknown within Claudius's reign.

events.title: Paul at Ephesus and the riot of the silversmiths
events.summary: Paul spent two to three years at Ephesus c. 52-55, writing letters to Corinth and probably Philippi and Philemon; Acts says his success caused the silversmith Demetrius, maker of silver shrines of Artemis, to raise a riot in which the crowd shouted "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians" in the theatre for two hours.
events.detail: The town clerk (grammateus) dispersed the crowd by warning of Roman action against an unlawful assembly, a detail consistent with Ephesian civic institutions known from inscriptions. Paul's letters mention "fighting with beasts at Ephesus" and an affliction in Asia so severe that he despaired of life, possibly imprisonment. The great theatre where the riot took place seated about 24,000.

events.title: Seneca's Apocolocyntosis
events.summary: Soon after Claudius's death in October 54 Seneca, who had delivered Nero's laudation of the deified emperor, wrote the Apocolocyntosis ("Pumpkinification"), a Menippean satire in prose and verse in which Claudius is refused admission to Olympus and condemned to play dice with a bottomless box and serve as a clerk in the underworld.
events.detail: The work mocks Claudius's limp, stammer, Gallic birth, passion for jurisdiction and execution of 35 senators and 221 knights. Dio mentions the title; the manuscripts call it Divi Claudii Apotheosis or Ludus de morte Claudii. It shows how quickly the new regime distanced itself from its predecessor even while maintaining his cult, which Nero soon neglected.

events.title: Seneca's De Clementia addressed to Nero
events.summary: In 55-56, after Nero's eighteenth birthday, Seneca addressed On Clemency to the young emperor, presenting mercy as the virtue that distinguishes a king from a tyrant and openly calling the princeps a king whose power over life and death is absolute.
events.detail: The treatise opens with Nero imagined saying "I alone of mortals have been chosen to act as gods on earth", and holds up Augustus's pardon of Cinna. It is the first theoretical statement of the Principate as monarchy in Latin. Written soon after the murder of Britannicus, it has been read either as sincere programme or as an attempt to bind Nero to his own early promises in his accession speech.

events.title: Nero proposes to abolish indirect taxes
events.summary: In 58, after complaints about the tax-farmers, Nero proposed abolishing all indirect taxes (vectigalia) as a gift to mankind; senators persuaded him that the empire could not survive without them, and instead he ordered the regulations of each tax to be published and limited the publicani's powers.
events.detail: Tacitus lists the reforms: claims older than a year lapsed, praetors and governors were to hear cases against publicani out of turn, soldiers kept their exemptions, and the 2.5% customs dues (quadragesima) and other duties stayed. The surviving customs law of Asia (Monumentum Ephesenum), revised in 62, reflects the same concern for published rules.

events.title: Arrest of Paul in Jerusalem and custody at Caesarea
events.summary: Bringing his collection for the poor to Jerusalem c. 57, Paul was attacked in the Temple on the charge of bringing a Gentile inside the sacred enclosure, rescued by the tribune Claudius Lysias and held for two years at Caesarea by the procurator Felix, who hoped for a bribe.
events.detail: Two Greek inscriptions found in Jerusalem warn foreigners not to pass the balustrade around the inner courts on pain of death, the charge against Paul. When Porcius Festus succeeded Felix (c. 59/60) and proposed trial in Jerusalem, Paul as a Roman citizen appealed to Caesar; Festus consulted Agrippa II and Berenice before sending him to Rome. The letter to the Romans, written from Corinth just before this journey, is Paul's most systematic theological statement.

events.title: Corbulo marches through Armenia to Tigranocerta
events.summary: After burning Artaxata in 58, Corbulo led his army in summer 59 across the parched uplands of Armenia to Tigranocerta, which opened its gates; he took the fortress of Legerda and in 60 installed Tigranes VI, a Cappadocian prince educated at Rome, as king.
events.detail: Tacitus describes the army living on meat and short of water, and the arrival at Tigranocerta of a Parthian noble's head catapulted into the camp of the defenders of Legerda. Tigranes, great-grandson of Herod and Archelaus of Cappadocia, proved reckless: his raid into Adiabene in 61 provoked Vologases to besiege him and reopen the war.

events.title: Nero founds the Neronia
events.summary: In 60 Nero instituted the Neronia, quinquennial Greek-style games in music, gymnastics and horsemanship, opening a gymnasium with free oil for senators and knights; at the second celebration (65) he performed on the lyre himself.
events.detail: The Juvenalia of 59, held privately in his gardens to celebrate the first shaving of his beard, had already brought senators and noblewomen onto the stage. Nero was given the prize for Latin oratory and verse at the first Neronia without competing, and the prize for lyre by acclamation. Tacitus records traditionalist outrage at the Greek nudity of the gymnasium. The games lapsed after his death but prepared the way for Domitian's Capitoline Games.

events.title: The comet of 60 and the fall of Rubellius Plautus
events.summary: A comet in 60, popularly believed to portend a change of ruler, led people to speculate about Rubellius Plautus, a great-grandson of Tiberius through his mother; Nero advised him to retire to his estates in Asia, where he was killed in 62.
events.detail: Tacitus mentions the comet with lightning that struck Nero's table at Sublaqueum. Seneca's Natural Questions (7.17, 7.21) discusses a comet visible "in the principate of Nero, which has rescued comets from disrepute". Another comet in 64 and Halley's comet in 66 were followed by more executions, according to Suetonius, who says the astrologer Balbillus advised Nero to divert the omen onto noble victims.

events.title: Earthquake destroys Laodicea on the Lycus
events.summary: An earthquake in 60 destroyed Laodicea in the Lycus valley, which Tacitus says rebuilt itself from its own resources without help from Rome.
events.detail: Tacitus contrasts Laodicea's self-sufficiency with the subsidies given to the Asian cities in 17. The city was a rich banking and textile centre; Revelation 3.17 has the church of Laodicea boasting "I am rich and need nothing". Colossae and Hierapolis nearby were probably also damaged.

events.title: The freedman Polyclitus investigates Britain
events.summary: After Boudica's defeat the procurator Julius Classicianus, at odds with Suetonius Paullinus's harsh reprisals, reported that there would be no end to the war under him; Nero sent his freedman Polyclitus with a large retinue to investigate, and Paullinus was soon replaced by the conciliatory Petronius Turpilianus.
events.detail: Tacitus enjoys the Britons' astonishment that a general who had won such a war obeyed slaves. Classicianus died in office; his tombstone, set up by his wife Julia Pacata, daughter of the Treveran Indus, was found in London in 1852 and 1935 and is in the British Museum. The episode marks the end of the conquest phase and a shift to consolidation.

events.title: Parthian siege of Tigranocerta and Corbulo's truce
events.summary: In 61 Vologases I sent Monaeses with cavalry and Adiabenian troops to besiege Tigranes VI in Tigranocerta; the Roman garrison held, and Corbulo's envoy secured a Parthian withdrawal and agreement that Tiridates's claim would be referred to Rome.
events.detail: Corbulo advised Nero to appoint a separate commander for Armenia; Caesennius Paetus arrived in 62 boasting he would impose provincial taxes, and soon capitulated at Rhandeia. Tacitus suspects that Corbulo preferred a truce that preserved his own reputation.

sides.strength: cavalry under Monaeses and Adiabenian troops

events.title: The customs law of Asia (Monumentum Ephesenum)
events.summary: A Greek inscription from Ephesus, discovered in 1976, preserves the customs law of the province of Asia as revised by a commission of three consulars in 62, with clauses going back to 75 BC.
events.detail: The text sets out the 2.5% duty (quadragesima) on goods entering or leaving the province, the list of customs stations, exemptions (for state property, soldiers' goods, items for religious use), the procedures for declaration and the rights of the publicani, with additions dated by consuls over 140 years. It is the most detailed document on Roman indirect taxation and illustrates the publication of tax rules Nero ordered in 58.

events.title: Stoning of James the brother of Jesus
events.summary: In the interval between the death of the procurator Festus and the arrival of Albinus in 62, the High Priest Ananus son of Ananus convened the Sanhedrin and had James "the brother of Jesus called Christ" and others stoned; Agrippa II deposed Ananus after three months.
events.detail: Josephus's brief notice, generally accepted as authentic, says the fair-minded citizens strict in the law protested to Agrippa and to Albinus. James had led the Jerusalem church for nearly twenty years and was revered as "the Just" for his Torah piety; Hegesippus (in Eusebius) gives a legendary account of his being thrown from the Temple pinnacle. His death removed the main bridge between the Jesus movement and Jerusalem's Jewish establishment.

events.title: Hero of Alexandria and the eclipse of 62
events.summary: Hero of Alexandria's Dioptra uses a lunar eclipse observed at Alexandria and Rome to compute the distance between the cities; the eclipse has been identified as that of 13 March 62, dating Hero, author of the Pneumatica with its steam-driven aeolipile and coin-operated holy water dispenser, to the mid first century.
events.detail: Otto Neugebauer's identification of the eclipse settled a dating controversy that had ranged from the third century BC to the third century AD. Hero's surviving works (Pneumatica, Automata, Mechanica, Metrica, Belopoeica, Dioptra) describe self-moving theatres, a programmable cart driven by a falling weight and string, a fire engine pump and surveying instruments, illustrating the sophistication and the limits of ancient mechanics.
events.debate: Some still question the identification of the eclipse.

events.title: Corbulo and Tiridates agree the settlement of Rhandeia
events.summary: In 63, after Corbulo invaded Armenia again with four legions, Tiridates met him at Rhandeia, site of Paetus's surrender, and laid his diadem before a statue of Nero, agreeing to receive it back from Nero's own hands in Rome.
events.detail: The compromise accepted an Arsacid king of Armenia as a Roman client, an arrangement that kept peace between Rome and Parthia for half a century until Trajan broke it in 114. Corbulo gave Tiridates his son-in-law Annius Vinicianus as escort. Tiridates left his daughter as hostage and made his famous three-year journey to Rome, avoiding the sea for religious reasons, for the coronation of 66. Nero closed the temple of Janus.

events.title: Annexation of the Cottian Alps
events.summary: On the death of king Cottius II, Nero converted his Alpine kingdom, centred on Segusio and the Mont Genevre pass, into a procuratorial province in 63, as he had annexed Pontus in 64.
events.detail: The dynasty of Donnus and Cottius had ruled as Roman prefects and kings since Augustus; Cottius I's arch at Segusio (9-8 BC) lists the fourteen communities under his rule. Claudius had enlarged the kingdom and restored the royal title in 44. The Maritime Alps had already received Latin rights from Nero.

events.title: Lucan's civil war epic and his quarrel with Nero
events.summary: Seneca's nephew Lucan (39-65) published the first three books of his De Bello Civili ("Pharsalia") c. 62-63 with a flattering dedication to Nero, but after a falling-out the emperor forbade him to publish or recite; the poem, an anti-Caesarian epic without gods, broke off in Book 10 when Lucan was forced to suicide for his part in the Pisonian conspiracy.
events.detail: Suetonius's Life of Lucan says Nero walked out of a reading, and that Lucan recited a line of Nero's own in a latrine. Lucan reputedly recited verses on a dying soldier as he bled to death. The poem's hero is Cato, its verdict on the Republic's fall bleak ("victrix causa deis placuit sed victa Catoni"). Statius wrote a birthday poem for his widow Polla Argentaria.

events.title: Seneca's Moral Letters to Lucilius
events.summary: In retirement after 62 Seneca wrote 124 Moral Letters to his friend Lucilius, procurator of Sicily, together with the Natural Questions, the most influential body of Stoic writing in Latin.
events.detail: The letters move from daily incidents (a trip in a tunnel at Naples, the noise above a bath-house, the treatment of slaves as "humble friends" in Letter 47) to ethical instruction. Letter 91 describes the fire that destroyed Lugdunum, and Letter 56 the din of a Baiae bath. The Natural Questions discuss the Campanian earthquake of 62, comets and the Nile. Seneca's apparent hypocrisy as a millionaire moralist, attacked by Suillius Rufus in 58, has shaped his reputation ever since.

events.title: Traditions of the deaths of Peter and Paul in Rome
events.summary: Early Christian tradition places the deaths of Peter, crucified, and Paul, beheaded, at Rome under Nero, probably in the persecution after the fire of 64 or a few years later; the earliest allusion is 1 Clement (c. 96).
events.detail: Around 200 the Roman presbyter Gaius pointed to the "trophies" of the apostles on the Vatican and on the road to Ostia (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 2.25). Excavations under St Peter's (1940-1949) found a small aedicula of c. 160 against the "red wall" in a pagan cemetery near Nero's circus, almost certainly Gaius's trophy; whether bones found nearby are Peter's is unprovable. Paul's execution is placed at Aquae Salviae (Tre Fontane), his tomb under San Paolo fuori le Mura. Dates of 64, 67 and 68 are all found.
events.locName: Vatican hill and Via Ostiensis, Rome
events.debate: No contemporary evidence for the manner or date; Peter's presence in Rome was once doubted but is now widely accepted.

events.title: Fire destroys Lugdunum
events.summary: A fire destroyed much of Lugdunum, capital of the Three Gauls, in a single night, probably in 64 or 65; Seneca wrote that "there was one night between a great city and none", and Nero sent four million sesterces, the sum Lugdunum had given Rome after the great fire.
events.detail: Tacitus records the gift under 65. The disaster made the city loyal to Nero in 68, when it refused to support Vindex and was besieged by the Viennenses. Seneca's Letter 91, consoling his friend Aebutius Liberalis, a native of the city, is the main description.

events.title: Pestilence and storm of 65
events.summary: In 65 a pestilence killed some 30,000 people at Rome (the number registered at the shrine of Libitina), without any visible change in the weather, while a hurricane devastated Campania.
events.detail: Tacitus lists the houses full of corpses and the streets full of funerals, with knights and senators dying alike. Suetonius gives the 30,000 figure in an autumn. The epidemic, of unknown nature, came in the year of the Pisonian purge, and Tacitus treats it as part of a catalogue of divine anger.

events.title: Condemnation of Thrasea Paetus and Barea Soranus
events.summary: In 66 Nero had the Stoic senator Thrasea Paetus, who had walked out of the Senate after Agrippina's murder and absented himself for three years, condemned along with Barea Soranus; Thrasea opened his veins in his garden, offering the blood as a libation "to Jupiter the Liberator".
events.detail: The accuser Cossutianus Capito compared Thrasea's followers to the partisans of Cato; Soranus's daughter Servilia was charged with consulting magicians for her father. Thrasea's son-in-law Helvidius Priscus was exiled. The surviving text of the Annals breaks off in the middle of Thrasea's death scene. Thrasea had written a Life of Cato, and his circle became the core of the "Stoic opposition" persecuted again under Vespasian and Domitian.

events.title: Nero plans an expedition to the Caspian Gates
events.summary: In 66-67 Nero planned an expedition to the "Caspian Gates" against the Alans, raising a new legion, I Italica, of Italian recruits six feet tall that he called the "phalanx of Alexander the Great", and moving troops from Germany, Britain and Illyricum eastwards.
events.detail: The objective was probably the Darial pass in the central Caucasus, which controlled the route of nomad raids into Armenia and Iberia, perhaps in cooperation with Parthia after the Rhandeia settlement. The Jewish revolt and the Vindex rising in 68 caused the plan to be dropped; detachments assembled for it were caught up in the civil war of 69.

events.title: Nero begins the Corinth canal
events.summary: During his tour of Greece Nero inaugurated a canal through the Isthmus of Corinth in 67, striking the first blow with a golden pickaxe; some 6,000 Jewish prisoners from Vespasian's campaign worked on it, but the project was abandoned on his death.
events.detail: Earlier schemes by Periander, Demetrius Poliorcetes and Caesar had been dropped. Nero's cuttings, about 2 km in all at both ends, were rediscovered when the modern canal (1881-1893) followed the same line. Egyptian engineers had reportedly warned that the Corinthian Gulf was higher than the Saronic and would flood Aegina. The diolkos tramway remained in use.

events.title: Columella's treatise on agriculture
events.summary: Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella of Gades wrote his twelve books On Agriculture c. 60-65, the fullest Roman manual of estate management, notable for its calculation of the profitability of vineyards and its complaint that Italian landowners neglected farming.
events.detail: Book 10 on gardens is in hexameters, continuing Virgil's Georgics. Columella's model vineyard (3.3) with its cost of land, slaves and vines and expected return, has been central to debates about whether Roman landowners thought in terms of investment and profit. He discusses the vilicus and slave management in detail and describes his uncle's experiments breeding African rams with Spanish ewes.

events.title: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea
events.summary: A Greek merchant's handbook of c. 40-70, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea describes ports, goods and rulers from Egypt's Red Sea harbours of Myos Hormos and Berenice along the African coast to Rhapta and across the Arabian Sea to the Indus, Barygaza, Muziris and the Ganges.
events.detail: The author lists exports (pepper, malabathrum, pearls, ivory, silk, cotton, incense) and imports demanded in India (wine, coral, glass, Roman coin). He credits Hippalus with discovering the direct monsoon crossing. Allusions to the Nabataean king Malichus II (40-70) and the Kushana and Satavahana rulers give the date. Pliny says India drained 50 million sesterces a year from the empire. Excavations at Berenike, Myos Hormos and Arikamedu confirm the trade.
events.locName: Red Sea and Indian Ocean (Adulis, Muziris)
